question: According to reports by AlgorithmWatch1, general-purpose AI chatbots across Europe blur the line between official health information and anti-abortion advocacy, directing users seeking information in cases of unwanted pregnancy to anti-abortion content without clearly identifying sources, including by failing to distinguish between official health authorities and anti-abortion organisations, making it difficult for users to assess the provenance and reliability of the information.
A team of female journalists tested ChatGPT-5 (OpenAI), Gemini 3 (Google), Grok 4.3 (xAI) and Claude Sonnet 4.8 (Anthropic).

In Italy and the UK, official sources were not consistently included in chatbot responses, while in Germany recommendations for help even misdirected people to anti-abortion ‘counselling’, despite the fact that official consultations with healthcare professionals are required locally for an abortion. 1.

Does the Commission agree that reliable healthcare information on abortion from official sources is essential to protect the health, safety and fundamental rights of people in Europe and, if so, does it agree that the general-purpose AI chatbots could pose a systemic risk under the AI Act and, in the case of ChatGPT, under the Digital Services Act?
Is the Commission aware of the AlgorithmWatch report? If so, what steps has it taken to investigate and address this issue?
What other steps is the Commission taking to address the reliability of information given by chatbots and even possible foreign influence via chatbots?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.11.2026) Access to reliable healthcare information is essential to the protection of the health, safety and fundamental rights of people within Europe, including freedom of expression and information.

To the extent that chatbots are involved in accessing such information, the AI Act1 and the Digital Services Act2 (DSA) are the key legislative instruments which the Commission has to ensure this protection. Many of the most widely used chatbots are currently built on general-purpose AI models with systemic risk.

Under the AI Act, the providers of such models must assess and mitigate the systemic risks posed by their models, which may include the dissemination of misleading or inaccurate healthcare information. The Commission is aware of the AlgorithmWatch investigation.

Whilst its findings alone do not establish the existence of a systemic risk under the AI Act, the Commission is engaged in regulatory dialogue with leading providers, including in relation to their post-market monitoring, and taking formal actions as needed.

Following designation of ChatGPT as a very large online search engine under the DSA, its provider will also be required from January 2027 to assess and mitigate systemic risks presented by it, including risks related to actual or foreseeable negative effects on the protection of public health and minors and serious negative consequences to physical and mental well-being.

The Commission is committed to using its full supervisory and enforcement powers to ensure compliance with both regulations. The European Democracy Shield also plays an important role in countering foreign information manipulation and interference and disinformation, with the safeguarding of the integrity of the information space as one of its three main pillars3.
1 Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and the Council of 13 June 2024 laying down

harmonised rules on artificial intelligence and amending Regulations (EC) No 300/2008, (EU) No 167/2013, (EU) No 168/2013, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2019/2144 and Directives 2014/90/EU, (EU) 2016/797 and (EU) 2020/1828 (AI Act). 2 Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 October 2022 on a Single Market For Digital Services and amending Directive 2000/31/EC.
